## Open

### F-171 — Party tap suite is fragile on data other suites leave behind

> _2026-09-16 · realm/blong-party · open_

test.acl.flow asserted exactly one person with lastName 'Doe', but the shared test database already
held a duplicate John Doe from another suite and the count assertion failed on data unrelated to the
change. Relaxed to 'at least one' for the duplicated name. Lesson: in a database shared by several
suites, never assert an exact count on a fixture that other suites can also create.

### F-172 — Playwright baseline pass found a behaviour question, not a screenshot diff

> _2026-09-16 · realm/blong-party · open_

T-096 was recorded as 're-baseline the party specs'. Running them showed 3 real failures
(organization/unit create + portal person browse) caused by the ACL guard hiding freshly created
records from their creator - not by stale screenshots. The blong-access suite (23 tests, including
the new ACL tabs and exceptions page) passes unchanged. Lesson: a guard that removes records from a
list breaks the shared create-and-verify model spec, so it must be decided before baselines are
touched.

### F-281 — The party specs assert after real round trips on a five-second budget

> _2026-09-26 · realm/blong-party · open_

Two CI failures in one run had the same shape: the flow worked and the UI had not caught up. The
registration spec's trace showed `access/registration/add` answering 200 in 2672ms and
`login/token/create` 200 in 2109ms, with `access/profile/get` still in flight when the five-second
expectation on `.blong-portal-menubar` expired — a time budget rather than a bug, since the suite
ran with Playwright's 5s expect default while these specs assert after real round trips;
`defineBlongConfig` now sets 15s there, and the Portal helpers keep failing fast because they pass
their own `BLONG_ELEMENT_TIMEOUT` for the missing-element case they are about. The flaky one is
worth remembering separately: the profile spec normalises the admin's name in the database _after_
the fixture has rendered the page, so the account menu kept the leftover initials — the trace's
`Received string: "TE"` where the spec wants `TA` — and the retry passed because the failed
attempt's own call had normalised the row by then; the spec now reloads after the normalisation,
which is the same state the retry starts from.

### F-282 — Concurrent local logins answered 500 from login/token/create

> _2026-09-26 · realm/blong-party · open_

A local run of this suite reported three tests flaky for one reason: `POST /rpc/login/token/create`
answered 500 and the auto-login fixture's menubar wait (its own `BLONG_ELEMENT_TIMEOUT`, five
seconds) expired; every one of them passed on retry. The pattern is worth recognising because it
looks like a suite fault and is not: four Playwright workers logging in together against the shared
dev database is what produces it, the same class as F-171, and it is invisible in a run whose retry
succeeds. It also nearly got blamed on a config change made in the same session — the entry already
passes `ci` in CI, so the db adapter's keep-alive and retry settings were the same before and after,
and a 500 comes from the server, not from an expectation budget. Look at the trace's network log
before suspecting the test.

### F-344 — belongsTo inherits roles in both directions

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · open_

belongsTo is an inheritance edge in both directions, so a role held by a unit reaches the persons in
it (the second branch of access_effectiveRolePath) and a unit inherits the roles and the ancestor
scopes of the organization it belongs to (the actor's principals include the units it belongs to). A
service-account fixture therefore cannot put a read-granting role on a unit whose members must stay
RBAC-forbidden, and an RBAC-forbidden account needs a node with no granted ancestor — which is why
the fixture gives the accounts their own roles and puts the forbidden row on the second
organization.

### F-345 — A unit record's scope set is its organization, not its isPartOf parent

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · open_

Two cells of the application matrix's unit table failed on the first run (axis-hq-app against North
and South expected allowed, observed denied). party.unit declares scopes: \['belongsTo'\] only, so
recordScopesSql in core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/acl.ts collects a unit's belongsTo target (its
organization) plus that organization's ancestry; the unit's own isPartOf parent is not a scope, and
the ancestry is resolved from the scope object rather than from the record. A grant naming a unit
therefore covers the persons inside it and no unit record at all. Only party.person widens through
isPartOf, via the unit a person belongsTo.

### F-349 — A fixture read owns its session and must be cached in the suite budget

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · open_

Two traps in the fixture step. The session belongs to whatever the previous step signed in as - a
matrix row leaves its viewer behind - so assuming testAdmin answered Authorization denied, while
signing in before every table costs about two seconds each; the helper now attempts the read and
signs in only when it is refused. And one read (login plus four queries) measures about three
seconds, which pushed the application feature past the tap budget once the same Background ran
before all three of its scenarios; caching the answer per names and predicates for the process
brought the suite from 174 seconds of the 180 second ceiling back to 130, of which the application
group alone is 90.

### F-350 — Stale seed leftovers are what the fixture tables catch

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · open_

The new tables failed on their first run for a reason worth keeping: matrixNorth held a capability
matrixPersonView that no seed in the repository declares, a leftover from an earlier iteration of
the fixture, and four users named Amy, Ben and so on existed next to the new lower-case ones -
matched case-insensitively by the utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation, so a login could resolve either.
Both were removed from the dev database with SQL (the capability with its triples, paths and
access_capability row; the users with their sessions, credentials, triples and paths). The lesson is
the one the assertion exists for: core.triple.merge is insert-ignore, so a fixture that changes
shape leaves edges behind, and only an equality assertion finds them.

### F-353 — The fixture read depended on whatever the last step signed in as

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · open_

The fixture Background runs before a scenario's rows, so the session belonged to the previous step:
the read was refused with method not allowed and the feature file looked broken. The helper now
attempts the read and signs in as the harness user only when it is refused, which is both correct
and cheaper, since a login costs about two seconds. It also caches the graph answer per names and
predicates for the process: one read (login plus four queries) measures about three seconds, and the
same Background runs before each of three scenarios, which pushed the tap file past its 180 second
ceiling before the cache existed (174 seconds total, 130 after).

### F-354 — A helper module in a handler group is logged as a load error

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · open_

Adding browser/test/test/aclSteps.ts as a plain module with named exports produced two Watch error
lines per run (probably a generic source code was put in a handler group folder) because the loader
gives every file in a handler group the shape of a handler. Turning it into a library fixed it and
is cheap: the factories are reached through lib like any other shared function. Five such files
predate this in other realms (gatewayUuid.ts, core.ts in blong-core, oidc.ts, account.ts and
accessModel.ts in blong-access) and each still logs the same error line on every run.

## Resolved

### F-340 — RBAC is unobservable from an in-process test call

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-party · resolved_

RBAC is enforced only at the HTTP gateway, as a Fastify preHandler in core/blong-gogo/src/jwt.ts; a
server-side in-process handler call skips the action check entirely, so a 403 cannot be observed
from a tap step. The existing test.acl.flow shows the symptom: a Customer-role caller with no grant
receives acl.notFound rather than 403. An RBAC assertion must therefore go through the gateway,
either as a browser-side HTTP flow or through an MLE session.

Addressed by the ACL matrix, which probes through the gateway (D-348) so RBAC and the record-level
ACL both decide a cell.
